entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12427"/><div sID="gen22797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12427"/><hi type="bold">2. Take with you words--</hi>instead of sacrifices, namely, the words of penitence here put in your mouths by God. "Words," in Hebrew, mean "realities," there being the same term for "words" and "things"; so God implies, He will not accept empty professions (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.36">Psa 78:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Is 29:13</reference>). He does not ask costly sacrifices, but words of heartfelt penitence.<div eID="gen22797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive us graciously--</hi>literally "(for) good."<div eID="gen22798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calves of our lips--</hi>that is, instead of sacrifices of calves, which we cannot offer to Thee in exile, we present the praises of our lips. Thus the exile, wherein the temple service ceased, prepared the way for the gospel time when the types of the animal sacrifices of the Old Testament being realized in Christ's perfect sacrifice once for all, "the sacrifice of praise to God continually that is the fruit of our lips" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">He 13:14</reference>) takes their place in the New Testament. <div eID="gen22799" type="x-p"/>

Three besetting sins of Israel are here renounced, trust in Assyria, application to Egypt for its cavalry (forbidden, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">Ho 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.5">11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.17">Psa 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Is 30:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">31:1</reference>), and idolatry.<div eID="gen22800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fatherless--</hi>descriptive of the destitute state of Israel, when severed from God, their true Father. God will not be "as the early dew that goeth away," but constant (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.19">Job 29:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.12">Pr 19:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lily--</hi>No plant is more productive than the lily, one root often producing fifty bulbs [Pliny, Natural History, 21.5]. The common lily is white, consisting of six leaves opening like bells. The royal lily grows to the height of three or four feet; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.29">Mt 6:29</reference> alludes to the beauty of its flowers.<div eID="gen22806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roots as Lebanon--</hi>that is, as the trees of Lebanon (especially the cedars), which cast down their roots as deeply as is their height upwards; so that they are immovable [Jerome], (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Is 10:34</reference>). Spiritual growth consists most in the growth of the root which is out of sight. <div eID="gen22807" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12432"/><div sID="gen22811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12432"/>7. They that used to dwell under Israel's shadow (but who shall have been forced to leave it), shall return, that is, be restored (<reference osisRef="Ezek.35.9">Eze 35:9</reference>). Others take "His shadow" to mean Jehovah's (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">91:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Is 4:6</reference>), which <reference osisRef="Hos.14.1">Ho 14:1</reference>, 2 ("return unto the Lord," &c.) favor. But the "his" in <reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">Ho 14:6</reference> refers to Israel, and therefore must refer to the same here.<div eID="gen22811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">revive as ... corn--</hi>As the corn long buried in the earth springs up, with an abundant produce, so shall they revive from their calamities, with a great increase of offspring (compare <reference osisRef="John.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference>).<div eID="gen22812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scent thereof--</hi>that is, Israel's fame. Compare <reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">Ho 14:6</reference>, "His smell as Lebanon"; <reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>: "Thy name is as ointment poured forth." The Septuagint favors the Margin, "memorial."<div eID="gen22813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the wine of Lebanon--</hi>which was most celebrated for its aroma, flavor, and medicinal restorative properties. <div eID="gen22814" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12433"/><div sID="gen22815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12433"/><hi type="bold">8. Ephraim shall say--</hi>being brought to penitence by God's goodness, and confessing and abhorring his past madness.<div eID="gen22815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have heard ... and observed him--</hi>I Jehovah have answered and regarded him with favor; the opposite of God's "hiding His face from" one (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">De 31:17</reference>). It is the experience of God's favor, in contrast to God's wrath heretofore, that leads Ephraim to abhor his past idolatry. Jehovah heard and answered: whereas the idols, as Ephraim now sees, could not hear, much less answer.<div eID="gen22816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am ... a green fir--</hi>or cypress; ever green, winter and summer alike; the leaves not falling off in winter.<div eID="gen22817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">From me is thy fruit found--</hi>"From Me," as the root. Thou needest go no farther than Me for the supply of all thy wants; not merely the protection implied by the shadow of the cypress, but that which the cypress has not, namely, fruit, all spiritual and temporal blessings. It may be also implied, that whatever spiritual graces Ephraim seeks for or may have, are not of themselves, but of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.4">Joh 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.8">5, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>). God's promises to us are more our security for mortifying sin than our promises to God (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Is 27:9</reference>). <div eID="gen22818" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 8. Ephraim shall say-- being brought to penitence by God's goodness, and confessing and abhorring his past madness. I have heard ... and observed him-- I Jehovah have answered and regarded him with favor; the opposite of God's "hiding His face from" one ( De 31:17 ). It is the experience of God's favor, in contrast to God's wrath heretofore, that leads Ephraim to abhor his past idolatry. Jehovah heard and answered: whereas the idols, as Ephraim now sees, could not hear, much less answer. I am ... a green fir-- or cypress; ever green, winter and summer alike; the leaves not falling off in winter. From me is thy fruit found-- "From Me," as the root. Thou needest go no farther than Me for the supply of all thy wants; not merely the protection implied by the shadow of the cypress, but that which the cypress has not, namely, fruit, all spiritual and temporal blessings. It may be also implied, that whatever spiritual graces Ephraim seeks for or may have, are not of themselves, but of God ( Psa 1:3 ; Joh 15:4 , 5, 8 ; Jas 1:17 ). God's promises to us are more our security for mortifying sin than our promises to God ( Is 27:9 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12434"/><div sID="gen22819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12434"/>9. Epilogue, summing up the whole previous teaching. Here alone Hosea uses the term "righteous," so rare were such characters in his day. There is enough of saving truth clear in God's Word to guide those humbly seeking salvation, and enough of difficulties to confound those who curiously seek them out, rather than practically seek salvation.<div eID="gen22819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall--</hi>stumble and are offended at difficulties opposed to their prejudices and lusts, or above their self-wise understanding (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.10.29">Pr 10:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.19">Mt 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Lu 2:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). To him who sincerely seeks the agenda, God will make plain the credenda. Christ is the foundation-stone to some: a stone of stumbling and rock of offense to others. The same sun softens wax and hardens clay. But their fall is the most fatal who fall in the ways of God, split on the Rock of ages, and suck poison out of the Balm of Gilead. <chapter eID="Hos.14"/><div eID="gen22820" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen22269" osisID="Hos" type="book"/>
